title: Claude Code Keeps Crashing? Try Switching to Warp Terminal
description: Endless scrolling, garbled text, memory failures... A different terminal can change your Claude Code workflow.
content_html:
If you have run Claude Code for a long time, this may sound familiar.

The first 10–20 minutes are fine, but as the conversation grows and output piles up...

  • The screen scrolls wildly and will not stop
  • As soon as you type, the view jumps upward and the input line disappears
  • Characters, especially Unicode and Korean text, appear garbled
  • In the worst cases, the IDE or even the OS crashes completely

These terminal and UI-rendering problems are reported fairly often in GitHub issues: endless scroll loops after long conversations, a frozen UI while the window is minimized, VS Code crashes caused by terminal-buffer redraws, JavaScript heap out of memory, and more.

This post explains **“how to improve Claude Code's perceived stability by moving it to Warp.”**

Why Can Changing the Terminal Help?

The problem may look like Claude Code's, but symptoms often become worse through its interaction with the terminal's rendering, scrollback, and reflow behavior. A TUI-based agent interface with long output and frequent updates can trigger buffer redraws, scrolling jumps, and CPU or memory spikes depending on the terminal implementation.

Warp is closer to a redesign of terminal UX along IDE lines than merely a “pretty terminal”:

  • It groups input and output into Blocks
  • The command input area works like a modern text editor
  • It has strong tab, pane, and session management, with multiple sessions built into its design

That structure changes how long output and extended sessions feel.

Installation: app.warp.dev

Is Login Required?

Login used to be strongly required, but the policy has changed so that basic features can now be used without logging in.

Managing Multiple Sessions: Split Panes + Tabs

The more Claude Code sessions you run at once, the more immediately useful Warp's split panes and tabs become.

It reminds me of the convenience of SecureCRT or PuTTY Connection Manager when managing several servers with PuTTY: organizing sessions into tabs, saving frequently used connections, and switching between terminals on one screen. Warp brings that feeling back to the local terminal.

Run 2–3 Claude Code Sessions with Split Panes

Warp can split a single tab into panes, each with its own terminal session.

ShortcutAction
CMD-DSplit right
Right-clickChoose a split direction
CMD-[ / CMD-]Move between panes

In each pane, navigate to the project folder and launch Claude Code. That is all.

Tip: assign one role to each pane. Left: analysis/planning; middle: implementation; right: tests/log monitoring.

Use Tabs to Separate Claude Code from General Work

Suggested setup:

  • Tab 1: 2–3 Claude Code panes
  • Tab 2: long-running tasks such as servers, logs, and DB tunnels
  • Tab 3: general shell work (git, grep, deployment, etc.)

Reduce Repetition with Autocomplete

Running multiple Claude Code sessions means repeating “navigate to the project folder → launch” dozens of times. Warp shortens that sequence.

Tab Completions

It suggests commands, options, and paths, and works over SSH too.

Autosuggestions

It automatically suggests commands based on shell history. Settings let you adjust behaviors such as accepting suggestions with Tab.

What you notice:

  • Suggestions appear as soon as you type cd
  • claude is immediately suggested from history too
  • Repeating the same work across sessions becomes faster

Notifications for Long-Running Tasks

If Claude Code changes something on the server during a task, or a development server exits unexpectedly, you may not notice immediately.

Warp provides desktop notifications:

  • When a command running longer than a specified duration finishes
  • When a running command asks for a password

You can immediately notice when a process such as npm run dev or docker compose up dies—that is, when the command exits.

Select and Copy Whole Blocks

Common tasks when working with Claude Code:

  • Copy and paste logs
  • Extract an error section for a follow-up question
  • Provide only a particular command's output as context

Warp groups input and output into Blocks, letting you:

  • Copy the command
  • Copy the output
  • Scroll straight to the start of the output

Dragging through long logs to select “just the part you need” is always error-prone, and even harder when the UI has bugs. Block-level copying solves that problem.

A File-System UI and Editing Inside the Terminal

File Tree

Open File Tree in the Tools panel on the left, and click a file to open it directly in Warp's code editor.

Right-click a file or folder to:

  • Open it in a new tab or pane
  • Copy its path
  • Attach it to the agent's context

Code Editor

Warp's built-in code editor provides:

  • Syntax highlighting
  • A tabbed file viewer
  • Find and replace
  • Vim keybindings

Instead of switching to an IDE to inspect files changed by Claude Code and then returning to the terminal, you get a workflow in which you make a quick edit inside Warp and immediately give the next instruction.

Reviewing Git Changes

When Claude Code edits several files, checking “What changed, and where?” can be painful.

Warp's Code Review panel supports:

  • Diff review
  • Apply, edit, or revert changes
  • Open files
  • Attach a diff to the agent's context

The structure is designed for flows such as reviewing an agent's changes, leaving feedback, and having it apply that feedback.

Remembering Each Tab's Folder Automatically

Working Directory Settings

You can choose the default directory for new sessions—windows, tabs, or panes:

  • Home directory
  • Previous session's directory (recommended)
  • Custom directory
  • Advanced (different settings for windows, tabs, and panes)

Recommended: “Previous session's directory.” New tabs and panes start directly in the current project directory.

Launch Configurations

A feature for saving a window, tab, and pane layout for each project and reopening it later exactly as it was.

Create a setup such as “three Claude Code panes + server tab + logs tab” once, and it is easy to restore whenever you open the project.

Pricing

For running Claude Code—that is, ordinary terminal use—starting with the free plan is often sufficient.

  • Free plan: a limited monthly AI credit allowance (150/month for the first 2 months, then 75/month)
  • Higher plans: more credits and features

Since you can start without logging in, the barrier to installing it and trying it out is low.

Things to Keep in Mind

Telemetry and Privacy

  • Warp uses Sentry for crash reporting and Rudderstack for app analytics
  • Telemetry can be disabled in settings; when disabled, console interactions are not stored on the server

Closing Thoughts: Who I Recommend It For

  • You run Claude Code for hours each day, especially in multiple sessions
  • You experience flickering, endless scrolling, garbled text, or crashes in VS Code's integrated terminal
  • You want to minimize context switching while copying logs, inspecting diffs, and making quick file edits

In those cases, Warp may feel close to a life-changing improvement for your Claude Code workflow.

At the very least, multiple panes, block copying, notifications, the file tree, and diff review can make the workflow feel like an entirely different tool.

Download Warp: https://app.warp.dev

Leave a comment if you have any questions!
